  <!-- Define styles -->
  <defs>
    <style>
      .title { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 24px; font-weight: bold; text-anchor: middle; fill: #333; }
      .subtitle { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 18px; font-weight: bold; text-anchor: middle; fill: #555; }
      .process-box { fill: #e0f7fa; stroke: #00796b; stroke-width: 1.5; rx: 8; ry: 8; }
      .process-text { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; text-anchor: middle; fill: #004d40; }
      .input-output { fill: #fff3e0; stroke: #ff8f00; stroke-width: 1.5; rx: 8; ry: 8; }
      .input-output-text { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; text-anchor: middle; fill: #e65100; }
      .decision { fill: #ffebee; stroke: #c62828; stroke-width: 1.5; }
      .decision-text { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 11px; text-anchor: middle; fill: #b71c1c; }
      .analysis-box { fill: #e8eaf6; stroke: #303f9f; stroke-width: 1.5; rx: 8; ry: 8; }
      .analysis-text { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; text-anchor: middle; fill: #1a237e; }
      .connector { stroke: #9e9e9e; stroke-width: 1.5; fill: none; }
      .arrow-head { fill: #9e9e9e; }
      .iteration-text { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 10px; fill: #757575; text-anchor: middle; }
      .section-bg { fill: #f5f5f5; rx: 15; ry: 15; }
    </style>
    <marker id="arrow" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="0" refY="3.5" orient="auto">
      <polygon points="0 0, 10 3.5, 0 7" class="arrow-head" />
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- Title -->
  <text x="500" y="40" class="title">S1-Bench Methodology Flowchart</text>

  <!-- Section Backgrounds -->
  <rect x="10" y="60" width="480" height="650" class="section-bg" />
  <rect x="510" y="60" width="480" height="650" class="section-bg" />

  <!-- Section Titles -->
  <text x="250" y="85" class="subtitle">S1-Bench Construction</text>
  <text x="750" y="85" class="subtitle">LRM Evaluation on S1-Bench</text>

  <!-- Column 1: S1-Bench Construction -->
  <g id="construction-workflow">
    <!-- Step 1: Input/Preparation -->
    <rect x="50" y="100" width="180" height="50" class="input-output"/>
    <text x="140" y="120" class="input-output-text">Input: Benchmark Surveys,</text>
    <text x="140" y="135" class="input-output-text">Define Simple Subcategories</text>

    <!-- Step 2: Generation -->
    <rect x="50" y="170" width="180" height="60" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="140" y="190" class="process-text">Initial Q&A Generation</text>
    <text x="140" y="205" class="process-text">(Generators + A Priori</text>
    <text x="140" y="220" class="process-text">Simplicity Constraints)</text>

    <!-- Step 3: Quality Assessment -->
    <rect x="50" y="250" width="180" height="60" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="140" y="270" class="process-text">Quality Assessment</text>
    <text x="140" y="285" class="process-text">(Annotators + Discriminators)</text>
    <text x="140" y="300" class="process-text">Check Clarity, Uniqueness</text>

    <!-- Step 4: Decision -->
    <path d="M 140 355 m -70 0 l 70 -40 l 70 40 l -70 40 z" class="decision"/>
    <text x="140" y="352" class="decision-text">Retain /</text>
    <text x="140" y="364" class="decision-text">Modify /</text>
    <text x="140" y="376" class="decision-text">Discard?</text>

    <!-- Step 5: A Posteriori Verification -->
    <rect x="270" y="280" width="180" height="60" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="360" y="300" class="process-text">A Posteriori Verification</text>
    <text x="360" y="315" class="process-text">(Validators: Small LLMs,</text>
    <text x="360" y="330" class="process-text">Multi-Temp Sampling)</text>

    <!-- Step 6: Correctness Evaluation -->
    <rect x="270" y="360" width="180" height="50" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="360" y="380" class="process-text">Correctness Evaluation</text>
    <text x="360" y="395" class="process-text">(Evaluator: GPT-4o)</text>

    <!-- Step 7: Decision -->
     <path d="M 360 455 m -70 0 l 70 -40 l 70 40 l -70 40 z" class="decision"/>
    <text x="360" y="452" class="decision-text">All Correct</text>
    <text x="360" y="464" class="decision-text">& Robust?</text>

    <!-- Step 8: Iterative Reduction -->
    <rect x="270" y="515" width="180" height="60" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="360" y="535" class="process-text">Iterative Difficulty</text>
    <text x="360" y="550" class="process-text">Reduction (Max 3)</text>
    <text x="360" y="565" class="process-text">(Modify Q&A)</text>

    <!-- Step 9: Output -->
    <rect x="270" y="600" width="180" height="50" class="input-output"/>
    <text x="360" y="625" class="input-output-text">Output: S1-Bench Dataset</text>

    <!-- Construction Connectors -->
    <line x1="140" y1="150" x2="140" y2="170" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="140" y1="230" x2="140" y2="250" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="140" y1="310" x2="140" y2="315" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="210" y1="355" x2="270" y2="310" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="245" y="340" class="iteration-text">Retain</text>
    <line x1="360" y1="340" x2="360" y2="360" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="360" y1="410" x2="360" y2="415" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="430" y1="455" x2="450" y2="455" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="450" y1="455" x2="450" y2="600" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="450" y1="600" x2="450" y2="625" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="450" y1="625" x2="450" y2="625" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="445" y="530" class="iteration-text">Yes</text>
    <line x1="360" y1="495" x2="360" y2="515" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="380" y="510" class="iteration-text">No</text>
    <line x1="270" y1="545" x2="250" y2="545" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="250" y1="545" x2="250" y2="200" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="250" y1="200" x2="230" y2="200" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="210" y="550" class="iteration-text">Loop (≤3 times)</text>
    <line x1="140" y1="395" x2="140" y2="420" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="140" y1="420" x2="40" y2="420" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="40" y1="420" x2="40" y2="200" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="40" y1="200" x2="50" y2="200" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="80" y="410" class="iteration-text">Modify</text>

  </g>

  <!-- Column 2: LRM Evaluation -->
  <g id="evaluation-workflow">
    <!-- Step 1: Input -->
    <rect x="550" y="100" width="180" height="50" class="input-output"/>
    <text x="640" y="120" class="input-output-text">Input: S1-Bench,</text>
    <text x="640" y="135" class="input-output-text">22 LRMs</text>

    <!-- Step 2: Configuration & Generation -->
    <rect x="550" y="170" width="180" height="60" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="640" y="190" class="process-text">Configure LRMs</text>
    <text x="640" y="205" class="process-text">(Greedy & Top-p)</text>
    <text x="640" y="220" class="process-text">Generate Responses</text>

    <!-- Step 3: Define Metrics -->
    <rect x="550" y="250" width="180" height="70" class="process-box"/>
    <text x="640" y="270" class="process-text">Define Evaluation Metrics:</text>
    <text x="640" y="285" class="process-text">- Format (S/L-Corr)</text>
    <text x="640" y="300" class="process-text">- Efficiency (ART)</text>
    <text x="640" y="315" class="process-text">- Accuracy (Pass@1, Acc@k)</text>

    <!-- Step 4: Main Results Analysis -->
    <rect x="550" y="340" width="180" height="60" class="analysis-box"/>
    <text x="640" y="360" class="analysis-text">Main Results Analysis</text>
    <text x="640" y="375" class="analysis-text">(Overthinking,</text>
    <text x="640" y="390" class="analysis-text">Under-accuracy)</text>

    <!-- Step 5: Detailed Analysis Group -->
    <rect x="770" y="170" width="190" height="370" class="analysis-box"/>
    <text x="865" y="190" class="analysis-text" style="font-weight:bold;">In-depth Analyses</text>

    <!-- Sub-Step 5a: Efficiency Analysis -->
    <rect x="780" y="210" width="170" height="90" fill="#c5cae9" rx="5" ry="5"/>
    <text x="865" y="230" class="analysis-text">Efficiency Analysis:</text>
    <text x="865" y="245" class="analysis-text">- ART by Question Type</text>
    <text x="865" y="260" class="analysis-text">- Solution Segmentation</text>
    <text x="865" y="275" class="analysis-text"> (Initial vs Additional Cost)</text>
    <text x="865" y="290" class="analysis-text">- Redundancy (Similarity)</text>

    <!-- Sub-Step 5b: Error Analysis -->
     <rect x="780" y="310" width="170" height="60" fill="#c5cae9" rx="5" ry="5"/>
    <text x="865" y="330" class="analysis-text">Error Analysis:</text>
    <text x="865" y="345" class="analysis-text">- Thinking Process (TP)</text>
    <text x="865" y="360" class="analysis-text"> vs Final Answer (FA)</text>

    <!-- Sub-Step 5c: Prejudgement Analysis -->
     <rect x="780" y="380" width="170" height="70" fill="#c5cae9" rx="5" ry="5"/>
    <text x="865" y="400" class="analysis-text">Simplicity Prejudgement:</text>
    <text x="865" y="415" class="analysis-text">- Identify Prejudgements</text>
    <text x="865" y="430" class="analysis-text">- Count Instances</text>
    <text x="865" y="445" class="analysis-text">- Compare ART</text>

    <!-- Step 6: Output Findings -->
    <rect x="660" y="560" width="180" height="70" class="input-output"/>
    <text x="750" y="580" class="input-output-text">Output: Key Findings</text>
    <text x="750" y="595" class="input-output-text">(LRM Inefficiency,</text>
    <text x="750" y="610" class="input-output-text">Under-accuracy,</text>
    <text x="750" y="625" class="input-output-text">Redundancy, Prejudgement)</text>

    <!-- Evaluation Connectors -->
    <line x1="640" y1="150" x2="640" y2="170" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="640" y1="230" x2="640" y2="250" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="640" y1="320" x2="640" y2="340" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <line x1="640" y1="400" x2="640" y2="420" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="640" y1="420" x2="770" y2="420" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="770" y1="420" x2="770" y2="355" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/> <!-- Connects Main Results to Detailed Analysis Box -->
     <line x1="865" y1="540" x2="865" y2="560" class="connector"/>
    <line x1="865" y1="560" x2="750" y2="560" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/> <!-- Connects Detailed Analysis to Output -->

  </g>

</svg>

title: Iterative Self-Training for Code Generation via Reinforced Re-Ranking
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper explores code generation using large language models with a novel reranking approach called RewardRanker.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The work builds upon previous code generation models and RLHF techniques, proposing a novel iterative self-training approach that uses Proximal Policy Optimization to improve reranking models rather than just generative models.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the challenge of generating high-quality code that solves complex programming tasks, particularly with decoder-based models that produce stochastic outputs where even minor errors can break entire solutions.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors developed an iterative self-training method combining supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, and PPO, with a cycle that incorporates hard negative examples into training to continuously improve reranking performance.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Their 13.4B parameter model outperformed a 33B parameter model while being three times faster, achieved performance comparable to GPT-4, and surpassed it in C++ programming language when evaluated on the MultiPL-E benchmark.

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of RewardRanker compared to traditional PPO approaches?
question1.option1: It focuses on optimizing the generative model with a reward model
question1.option2: It emphasizes developing a robust reward/reranking model rather than just the generative model
question1.option3: It eliminates the need for any reward model in code generation

question2.question: What key component makes the iterative self-training cycle of RewardRanker particularly effective?
question2.option1: The inclusion of hard negative examples in the training dataset
question2.option2: The exclusive use of correct solutions in training
question2.option3: Pre-defined test cases during inference

question3.question: How did the 13.4B parameter RewardRanker model compare to larger models in the evaluation?
question3.option1: It performed significantly worse but was much faster
question3.option2: It matched performance but required more computational resources
question3.option3: It outperformed a 33B model while being three times faster

<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 1000 800" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

  <!-- Define styles and gradients -->
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="grad1" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(150,200,255);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(100,150,255);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="grad2" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(255,200,150);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(255,150,100);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
     <linearGradient id="grad3" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(150,255,150);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(100,230,100);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
     <linearGradient id="grad4" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(255,180,220);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(230,150,200);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
     <linearGradient id="grad5" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(200,200,200);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(170,170,170);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
     <linearGradient id="grad6" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:rgb(255,230,130);stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:rgb(255,210,100);stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
    <marker id="arrowhead" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="0" refY="3.5" orient="auto">
      <polygon points="0 0, 10 3.5, 0 7" fill="#555" />
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- Title -->
  <text x="500" y="40" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">
    Iterative Self-Training for Code Generation via Reinforced Re-Ranking
  </text>
  <text x="500" y="65" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#666">
    Methodology Flowchart (RewardRanker)
  </text>

  <!-- Step 1: Initial Datasets -->
  <rect x="50" y="100" rx="10" ry="10" width="200" height="100" fill="url(#grad5)" stroke="#aaa" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="150" y="140" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Prepare Initial Datasets</text>
  <text x="150" y="160" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">- SFT Data (Prompt-Completion)</text>
  <text x="150" y="175" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">- Alignment Data (Triplets)</text>

  <!-- Step 2: SFT -->
  <rect x="350" y="100" rx="10" ry="10" width="300" height="100" fill="url(#grad1)" stroke="#88aaff" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="500" y="135" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">(A) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)</text>
  <text x="500" y="160" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Fine-tune base Generator Model</text>
  <text x="500" y="175" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">using SFT dataset.</text>

  <!-- Step 3: Train Reward Model -->
  <rect x="350" y="250" rx="10" ry="10" width="300" height="100" fill="url(#grad2)" stroke="#ffaa88" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="500" y="285" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">(B) Train RewardRanker</text>
  <text x="500" y="310" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Train Reranker/Reward Model</text>
  <text x="500" y="325" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">using Alignment Triplets.</text>

  <!-- Step 4: PPO Training -->
  <rect x="350" y="400" rx="10" ry="10" width="300" height="100" fill="url(#grad3)" stroke="#88ff88" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="500" y="435" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">(C) Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)</text>
  <text x="500" y="460" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Train Generator (from SFT)</text>
  <text x="500" y="475" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">using RewardRanker for rewards.</text>

  <!-- Step 5: Generate & Evaluate -->
  <rect x="350" y="550" rx="10" ry="10" width="300" height="120" fill="url(#grad4)" stroke="#ffaac0" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="500" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">(D) Generate & Evaluate New Examples</text>
  <text x="500" y="605" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Use PPO-trained Generator to create solutions.</text>
  <text x="500" y="620" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Evaluate with test cases.</text>
  <text x="500" y="635" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Identify: Positive Examples</text>
  <text x="500" y="650" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold" fill="#D32F2F">Identify: Hard Negative Examples</text>

  <!-- Step 6: Update Dataset -->
   <ellipse cx="150" cy="450" rx="100" ry="50" fill="url(#grad6)" stroke="#ffd282" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="150" y="440" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">(E) Refine Dataset</text>
  <text x="150" y="460" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Add generated Positive &</text>
   <text x="150" y="475" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold" fill="#D32F2F">Hard Negative examples</text>
   <text x="150" y="490" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">to Alignment Dataset.</text>


  <!-- Arrows / Connections -->
  <line x1="250" y1="150" x2="350" y2="150" stroke="#555" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>
  <line x1="500" y1="200" x2="500" y2="250" stroke="#555" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>
  <line x1="500" y1="350" x2="500" y2="400" stroke="#555" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>
  <line x1="500" y1="500" x2="500" y2="550" stroke="#555" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>

  <!-- Iteration Loop -->
  <path d="M 350 610 Q 250 610 200 550 Q 150 490 150 400" stroke="#555" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)"/>
  <text x="250" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#555">Generated Examples</text>

  <path d="M 150 395 L 150 325 Q 150 275 350 300" stroke="#D32F2F" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#arrowhead)" stroke-dasharray="5,5"/>
   <text x="220" y="270" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#D32F2F" font-weight="bold">Iterative Refinement Loop</text>
   <text x="220" y="290" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#D32F2F">(Feed refined dataset back to RewardRanker Training)</text>


  <!-- Annotations -->
   <rect x="700" y="100" rx="5" ry="5" width="250" height="60" fill="#f0f8ff" stroke="#add8e6" stroke-width="1"/>
   <text x="825" y="125" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">SFT prepares the generator</text>
   <text x="825" y="140" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">for domain-specific tasks.</text>

   <rect x="700" y="250" rx="5" ry="5" width="250" height="70" fill="#fff0f0" stroke="#ffc0cb" stroke-width="1"/>
   <text x="825" y="275" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">RewardRanker learns to</text>
   <text x="825" y="290" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">prefer correct over incorrect</text>
   <text x="825" y="305" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">code via pairwise comparison.</text>

   <rect x="700" y="400" rx="5" ry="5" width="250" height="70" fill="#f0fff0" stroke="#90ee90" stroke-width="1"/>
   <text x="825" y="425" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">PPO optimizes the generator</text>
   <text x="825" y="440" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">to maximize scores from the</text>
   <text x="825" y="455" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">current RewardRanker.</text>

   <rect x="700" y="550" rx="5" ry="5" width="250" height="70" fill="#fff5ee" stroke="#ffdab9" stroke-width="1"/>
   <text x="825" y="575" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">Crucial step: Identify</text>
   <text x="825" y="590" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold" fill="#D32F2F">'Hard Negatives'</text>
   <text x="825" y="605" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">(high-scoring failures).</text>

</svg>

title:
SocioVerse: A World Model for Social Simulation Powered by LLM Agents
  and A Pool of 10 Million Real-World Users
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces SocioVerse, a world model framework for social simulation using LLM-based agents to model human behavior across political, news, and economic domains.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on prior social simulation research but proposes a comprehensive framework with four alignment components (social environment, user engine, scenario engine, and behavior engine) and a 10-million real user pool to enhance simulation realism.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses alignment challenges between simulated environments and the real world, including maintaining up-to-date context, precisely modeling target users, aligning interaction mechanisms, and capturing diverse behavioral patterns.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors implemented the framework with a 10-million user pool from social media platforms, demographic annotation systems, and standardized simulation pipelines across three scenarios: presidential election prediction, breaking news feedback, and national economic surveys.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Results demonstrated that SocioVerse can accurately reflect large-scale population dynamics with over 90% accuracy in election predictions, consistent user reactions to breaking news, and close alignment with real-world economic statistics, while showing that both prior distribution and real-world knowledge enhance simulation accuracy.

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of SocioVerse compared to previous social simulation approaches?
question1.option1: It uses more powerful LLMs than previous approaches
question1.option2: It incorporates a 10-million real user pool with four alignment components
question1.option3: It focuses exclusively on political simulations

question2.question: In the presidential election prediction simulation, which factor had the most significant impact on improving accuracy?
question2.option1: The choice of underlying LLM model
question2.option2: The social environment's real-world knowledge
question2.option3: The prior demographics distribution of users

question3.question: What interesting pattern was observed about LLM performance in the national economic survey?
question3.option1: All models performed best on housing spending and worst on daily necessities
question3.option2: Models showed inconsistent performance across different spending categories
question3.option3: All models performed best on daily necessities spending and worst on housing spending

title: Seedream 3.0 Technical Report
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper presents Seedream 3.0, a high-performance Chinese-English bilingual image generation foundation model in the domain of AI-generated imagery.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds upon Seedream 2.0 while proposing new techniques including defect-aware training, dual-axis collaborative data sampling, mixed-resolution training, cross-modality RoPE, and novel acceleration methods.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve limitations in Seedream 2.0 including alignment with complicated prompts, fine-grained typography generation, suboptimal visual aesthetics, and limited image resolutions.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors employed improvements across the entire pipeline including doubling the dataset size, implementing mixed-resolution training, using cross-modality RoPE, applying representation alignment loss, and developing a novel acceleration paradigm with consistent noise expectation.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Seedream 3.0 demonstrates significant improvements over previous models, ranking first on the Artificial Analysis Text to Image Model Leaderboard with superior performance in text rendering (especially Chinese characters), photorealistic portrait generation, and native high-resolution output (up to 2K).

question1.question: What innovative approach did Seedream 3.0 use to expand its training dataset while maintaining quality?
question1.option1: Synthetic data generation using GANs
question1.option2: Defect-aware training with mask latent space optimization
question1.option3: Crowdsourced human annotation of all training images

question2.question: What is the primary technical advancement that allows Seedream 3.0 to achieve a 4 to 8 times speedup during inference?
question2.option1: Mixed-resolution training and cross-modality RoPE
question2.option2: Consistent noise expectation and importance-aware timestep sampling
question2.option3: VLM-based reward model with scaling

question3.question: In which capability area does Seedream 3.0 particularly excel compared to other leading models like GPT-4o?
question3.option1: Chinese text rendering and typography generation
question3.option2: 3D object generation with accurate physics
question3.option3: Multi-round image editing capabilities

title: TextArena
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces TextArena, a framework for evaluating large language models through competitive text-based games that assess social skills and agentic behavior.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on existing game-based evaluation frameworks but uniquely offers a comprehensive collection of 57+ text-based games with online evaluation capabilities, addressing limitations of traditional benchmarks that fail to assess dynamic social skills.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper solves the problem of evaluating complex social and strategic capabilities in language models that traditional benchmarks miss, such as negotiation, theory of mind, and deception.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors created a Gym-compatible framework with diverse text-based games (single/multi-player), implemented online evaluation using TrueSkill™ ratings, and developed a system for model-vs-model and model-vs-human competitions.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** The results show comparative performance of various language models across different soft skills (like strategic planning, theory of mind, and bluffing), with preliminary rankings displayed on a public leaderboard that includes both frontier models and community submissions.

question1.question: What is the primary advantage of TextArena's relative evaluation approach compared to traditional benchmarks?
question1.option1: It eliminates the need for human evaluation entirely
question1.option2: It has no clear upper limit of performance that can be reached
question1.option3: It focuses exclusively on single-player environments

question2.question: Which skill assessment methodology does TextArena use to rank models on its leaderboard?
question2.option1: Elo rating system with manual adjustments
question2.option2: Simple win/loss percentage calculations
question2.option3: TrueSkill™ bayesian skill rating system

question3.question: What unique capability does TextArena offer that most other game-based LLM evaluation frameworks lack?
question3.option1: Support for both model-vs-model and model-vs-human evaluation
question3.option2: The ability to test only strategic planning skills
question3.option3: A focus exclusively on two-player competitive games

title: Pixel-SAIL: Single Transformer For Pixel-Grounded Understanding
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces Pixel-SAIL, a single transformer architecture for pixel-grounded multimodal understanding tasks in computer vision and natural language processing.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on recent SAIL (Single trAnsformer as a unified vIsion-Language Model) designs but extends them to pixel-level understanding tasks, proposing a simplified architecture without the multiple components (vision encoders, segmentation experts) used in current MLLMs.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the high complexity of current Multimodal Large Language Models for pixel-level understanding tasks, which rely on multiple specialized components that limit model scaling and efficiency.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors propose three key improvements: a learnable upsampling module for visual token features, a novel visual prompt injection strategy, and a vision expert distillation strategy to enhance fine-grained feature extraction capabilities.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Pixel-SAIL achieves comparable or better results than state-of-the-art MLLMs on referring segmentation benchmarks, with the 3B model outperforming larger 7B models, while also introducing a new benchmark (PerBench) for comprehensive pixel understanding evaluation.

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of Pixel-SAIL compared to previous multimodal models?
question1.option1: It uses a much larger transformer with billions more parameters
question1.option2: It employs a single transformer architecture without additional vision encoders or segmentation experts
question1.option3: It focuses exclusively on text understanding while ignoring visual inputs

question2.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three technical improvements proposed in Pixel-SAIL?
question2.option1: A learnable upsampling module for visual token features
question2.option2: A specialized contrastive learning framework for text-image alignment
question2.option3: A vision expert distillation strategy to enhance feature extraction

question3.question: What is PerBench, as described in the paper?
question3.option1: A hardware benchmark for measuring transformer efficiency
question3.option2: A new comprehensive benchmark for pixel-understanding that includes detailed object description, visual prompt-based QA, and visual-text referring segmentation
question3.option3: A training methodology that periodically evaluates model performance

title: BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper presents BitNet b1.58 2B4T, the first open-source native 1-bit Large Language Model (LLM) with 2 billion parameters trained on 4 trillion tokens.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous quantization work but advances by creating a native 1-bit model trained from scratch rather than applying post-training quantization to existing models.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the computational inefficiency of current LLMs which require substantial memory, energy, and processing resources that limit their deployment in resource-constrained environments.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors trained a 2-billion parameter model from scratch using BitLinear layers with 1.58-bit weight quantization (ternary values), 8-bit activation quantization, and specialized training techniques including a two-stage learning rate schedule.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** BitNet b1.58 2B4T achieved performance comparable to leading open-weight full-precision models of similar size across multiple benchmarks while offering significantly reduced memory footprint (0.4GB vs 1.4-4.8GB), lower energy consumption, and faster inference speeds.

question1.option1: It was trained from scratch as a native 1-bit model rather than using post-training quantization
question1.option2: It uses a larger token dataset than any previous language model
question1.option3: It combines multiple smaller models into one efficient architecture

question2.question: What activation function does BitNet b1.58 2B4T use in its feed-forward network?
question2.option1: SwiGLU
question2.option2: Squared ReLU (ReLU²)
question2.option3: Sigmoid

question3.question: What is the memory footprint of BitNet b1.58 2B4T compared to other models of similar size?
question3.option1: About half the size of comparable models
question3.option2: Roughly the same size but with faster processing
question3.option3: Significantly smaller (0.4GB vs 1.4-4.8GB for comparable models)

title: Cobra: Efficient Line Art COlorization with BRoAder References
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper presents Cobra, an efficient framework for line art colorization in comic production, focusing on the domain of computer vision and image processing.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous reference-based colorization methods like ColorFlow but introduces novel innovations including Causal Sparse DiT architecture, Localized Reusable Position Encoding, and efficient attention mechanisms for handling extensive reference images.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the challenge of efficiently colorizing comic line art with high accuracy, contextual consistency, and flexible control while effectively handling numerous reference images.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors developed a framework featuring Causal Sparse Attention with KV-Cache to reduce computational complexity, Localized Reusable Position Encoding to handle arbitrary reference counts, and a Line Art Guider with style augmentation for robust colorization.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** The results show Cobra outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics (CLIP-IS, FID, PSNR, SSIM, and Aesthetic Score), achieving higher quality colorization with significantly faster inference time while supporting over 200 reference images.

question1.question: What is the main innovation in Cobra's attention mechanism that significantly reduces computational complexity?
question1.option1: Self-Attention-Only Block
question1.option2: Causal Sparse Attention with KV-Cache
question1.option3: Hint Point Sampling Strategy

question2.question: Why is Localized Reusable Position Encoding important in Cobra's architecture?
question2.option1: It improves the aesthetic quality of colorized images
question2.option2: It enables the integration of arbitrary numbers of reference images without modifying existing 2D position encodings
question2.option3: It helps extract line art from colored images

question3.question: What was demonstrated in the ablation study regarding reference image count?
question3.option1: More reference images actually decreased colorization quality due to noise
question3.option2: The optimal number of reference images was exactly 12 for all scenarios
question3.option3: Increasing the number of reference images improved colorization accuracy, especially for preserving small but important details

title: Heimdall: test-time scaling on the generative verification
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper focuses on developing a verification system for AI-generated solutions to complex problems, particularly in the domain of competitive mathematics.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on Chain-of-Thought reasoning approaches but addresses the underexplored area of verification capabilities in large language models; it proposes "Heimdall," a specialized verifier model trained through reinforcement learning.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the weak verification ability of current LLMs when checking complex mathematical solutions, which limits their ability to create and maintain reliable knowledge.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning with carefully filtered training data to train a long-context verification model, and propose "Pessimistic Verification" to optimize solution selection at inference time.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Heimdall achieved 94.5% verification accuracy on competitive math problems (increasing to 97.5% with scaled sampling), demonstrated strong generalization to math proofs, and when used with their Pessimistic Verification algorithm, improved solution accuracy on AIME2025 from 54.2% to 83.3% with sufficient compute budget.

question1.option1: It uses human experts to verify solutions before deployment
question1.option2: It leverages long Chain-of-Thought reasoning with reinforcement learning for verification
question1.option3: It relies on majority voting from multiple general-purpose LLMs

question2.question: What key data filtering strategy improved Heimdall's verification performance during training?
question2.option1: Removing problems with only correct solutions or only incorrect solutions
question2.option2: Focusing exclusively on AIME competition problems
question2.option3: Using only solutions from the strongest available solver models

question3.question: What did the authors discover when applying Heimdall to verify the NuminaMath synthetic dataset?
question3.option1: The dataset was nearly perfect with only minor errors
question3.option2: Nearly half of the dataset contained flaws, aligning with NuminaMath's own findings
question3.option3: Heimdall struggled to verify the dataset due to domain mismatch

  <circle cx="100" cy="590" r="10" style="fill:url(#grad2); stroke:#333;"/>

  <circle cx="100" cy="620" r="10" style="fill:url(#grad3); stroke:#333;"/>

title:
CLIMB: CLustering-based Iterative Data Mixture Bootstrapping for
  Language Model Pre-training
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces CLIMB, a framework for optimizing data mixtures for language model pre-training through clustering-based iterative bootstrapping.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous data mixture approaches but proposes a novel method to automatically identify, evaluate, and refine data mixtures without relying on predefined domain labels.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the challenge of finding optimal pre-training data mixtures for language models when working with large-scale web datasets that lack inherent domain divisions.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors cluster documents in semantic space, then iteratively optimize mixture weights using a bootstrapping process with proxy models and predictors to progressively refine the data mixture.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Using the optimal data mixture, their 1B model exceeded state-of-the-art Llama-3.2-1B by 2.0% on reasoning tasks, with domain-specific optimization yielding 5% improvement over random sampling; they also released ClimbLab and ClimbMix datasets.

question1.question: What is the main innovation of CLIMB compared to previous data mixture methods?
question1.option1: It uses larger proxy models to evaluate data quality
question1.option2: It automatically identifies and optimizes data mixtures without relying on predefined domain labels
question1.option3: It focuses exclusively on reasoning tasks rather than general capabilities

question2.question: In the CLIMB framework, what is the purpose of the iterative bootstrapping process?
question2.option1: To train increasingly larger language models at each iteration
question2.option2: To gradually filter out low-quality web content
question2.option3: To progressively refine the search space and eliminate suboptimal data mixture candidates

question3.question: What was a key finding from the ablation studies on CLIMB?
question3.option1: Using a 62M proxy model performed better than using a 350M proxy model
question3.option2: More search iterations improved performance, but compute should be balanced between depth and breadth
question3.option3: Random initialization consistently outperformed Dirichlet initialization

title:
Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in
  LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper examines whether reinforcement learning (RL) actually creates new reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs) beyond what exists in base models, focusing on mathematical, programming, and visual reasoning tasks.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous research in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) but challenges the common belief that RLVR enables LLMs to develop novel reasoning abilities beyond their base models.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to determine whether RLVR training genuinely introduces new reasoning capabilities to LLMs or merely optimizes existing capabilities from the base model.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors used the pass@k metric with large k values across multiple model families and benchmarks to measure the reasoning capability boundaries of both base and RL-trained models, combined with perplexity analysis.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** The results showed that while RL-trained models outperform base models at small k values, base models achieve higher pass@k scores at large k values, indicating that RLVR improves sampling efficiency but does not introduce new reasoning abilities beyond what already exists in the base models.

question1.question: According to the paper, what is the primary effect of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) on LLMs?
question1.option1: It creates entirely new reasoning capabilities beyond what exists in the base model
question1.option2: It improves sampling efficiency by biasing the model toward rewarded reasoning paths
question1.option3: It increases the model's ability to explore novel reasoning patterns

question2.question: What surprising phenomenon did the researchers observe when comparing base models to RL-trained models at large k values?
question2.option1: Base models consistently outperformed their RL-trained counterparts
question2.option2: Both models performed equally well regardless of k value
question2.option3: RL-trained models showed exponential improvement as k increased

question3.question: How does the paper distinguish between the effects of RLVR and distillation on LLM reasoning capabilities?
question3.option1: RLVR and distillation both reduce the model's reasoning boundary in similar ways
question3.option2: RLVR is bounded by the base model's capabilities, while distillation can genuinely introduce new knowledge
question3.option3: Distillation improves sampling efficiency while RLVR expands reasoning patterns

  <rect x="150" y="140" width="700" height="100" rx="10" ry="10" fill="url(#grad1)" class="box"/>

  <text x="500" y="190" text-anchor="middle" class="method">Proposed Method: Evaluate Reasoning Boundary using pass@k with LARGE k.</text>
  <text x="500" y="210" text-anchor="middle" class="detail">(Rationale: If Base Model solves problems with enough samples (large k),</text>
  <text x="500" y="225" text-anchor="middle" class="detail">the capability might already exist, just less efficiently sampled.)</text>

  <text x="100" y="340" class="detail">- LLaMA-3.1-8B</text>
  <text x="100" y="355" class="detail">- Qwen-2.5-VL-7B</text>

  <text x="350" y="310" class="sub-method">Tasks & Benchmarks:</text>
  <text x="350" y="325" class="detail">- Math: GSM8K, MATH500, Minerva, Olympiad, AIME24, AMC23</text>
  <text x="350" y="340" class="detail">- Code: LiveCodeBench, HumanEval+, MBPP+</text>
  <text x="350" y="355" class="detail">- Visual Reasoning: MathVista (filtered), MathVision (filtered)</text>

  <text x="700" y="340" class="detail">- Algorithms: GRPO (main), PPO, etc. (later analysis)</text>
  <text x="700" y="355" class="detail">- Evaluation: Zero-shot prompts, T=0.6, Top-p=0.95, large k (e.g., 256, 1024)</text>
  <text x="500" y="380" class="sub-method">Key Measurement: Plot pass@k curves for Base vs. RLVR models.</text>
  <line x1="500" y1="240" x2="500" y2="260" class="connector" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>

  <!-- Deep Analysis Section -->

  <g transform="translate(0, 450)">

    <text x="40" y="55" class="detail">Method:</text>
    <text x="50" y="70" class="detail">- Filter guessable problems (AIME24).</text>
    <text x="50" y="85" class="detail">- Manually inspect CoTs for hardest</text>
    <text x="50" y="100" class="detail">  problems solved at large k.</text>

    <!-- Analysis 2: Coverage & Perplexity -->
    <rect x="360" y="0" width="280" height="110" class="analysis-box" fill="url(#grad3)"/>
    <text x="500" y="20" text-anchor="middle" class="sub-method">2. Coverage & Perplexity Analysis</text>
    <text x="370" y="40" class="detail">Method 1: Solvable Set Comparison</text>
    <text x="380" y="55" class="detail">- Check if {Problems solved by RL} ⊆</text>
    <text x="380" y="70" class="detail">  {Problems solved by Base} at large k.</text>
    <text x="370" y="85" class="detail">Method 2: Perplexity</text>
    <text x="380" y="100" class="detail">- Calculate PPL_Base(Y_RL) vs PPL_Base(Y_Base).</text>

    <!-- Analysis 3: Distillation -->
    <rect x="690" y="0" width="280" height="110" class="analysis-box" fill="url(#grad3)"/>
    <text x="830" y="20" text-anchor="middle" class="sub-method">3. Comparison with Distillation</text>
    <text x="700" y="40" class="detail">Question: Does distillation behave differently?</text>
    <text x="700" y="55" class="detail">Method:</text>
    <text x="710" y="70" class="detail">- Compare pass@k curves of Base vs. RL</text>
    <text x="710" y="85" class="detail">  vs. Distilled Model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1</text>
    <text x="710" y="100" class="detail">  distilled into Qwen).</text>

    <!-- Analysis 4: RL Algorithms -->
    <rect x="30" y="130" width="450" height="130" class="analysis-box" fill="url(#grad3)"/>
    <text x="255" y="150" text-anchor="middle" class="sub-method">4. RL Algorithm & Training Step Analysis</text>
    <text x="40" y="170" class="detail">Method 1: Algorithm Comparison</text>
    <text x="50" y="185" class="detail">- Use VeRL framework for fair comparison (PPO, GRPO, RLOO...).</text>
    <text x="50" y="200" class="detail">- Define Sampling Efficiency Gap (ΔSE) = pass@k(Base) - pass@1(RL).</text>
    <text x="50" y="215" class="detail">- Evaluate on Omni-MATH splits.</text>
    <text x="40" y="230" class="detail">Method 2: Training Steps</text>
    <text x="50" y="245" class="detail">- Track pass@1 and pass@k(large) vs. training steps.</text>

    <!-- Link to Overall Goal -->
    <rect x="510" y="130" width="460" height="130" class="analysis-box" fill="url(#grad4)"/>
    <text x="740" y="150" text-anchor="middle" class="sub-method">Connecting Analyses to Research Question</text>

title: Antidistillation Sampling
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces "Antidistillation Sampling," a technique in AI security that prevents language models from being effectively distilled while maintaining their functionality.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on prior work in model distillation and data poisoning, proposing a novel approach to strategically modify a model's token probability distributions to resist distillation.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the problem of protecting proprietary large language models from being easily distilled by competitors who could use the models' reasoning traces to train their own systems at much lower cost.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use a gradient-based approach that modifies the sampling distribution by adding a penalty term based on a directional derivative capturing how token choices would impact a distilled model's performance, implemented efficiently using a finite-difference approximation.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Results show that antidistillation sampling successfully reduces student model performance (24.73% vs 51.86% on GSM8K) while maintaining comparable teacher model accuracy (68.51% vs 68.90%), demonstrating effective protection against distillation attempts.

question1.question: What is the primary goal of antidistillation sampling?
question1.option1: To improve the accuracy of language models on reasoning tasks
question1.option2: To protect proprietary models by preventing effective distillation while maintaining model utility
question1.option3: To reduce the computational cost of training large language models

question2.question: How does antidistillation sampling technically work?
question2.option1: By completely hiding token probabilities from model outputs
question2.option2: By adding random noise to the sampling distribution
question2.option3: By adding a penalty term based on the directional derivative of student model performance

question3.question: In the GSM8K benchmark experiments, what was demonstrated about antidistillation sampling?
question3.option1: It improved both teacher and student model performance
question3.option2: It maintained teacher accuracy around 68% while reducing student accuracy to about 25% (compared to 52% with temperature sampling)
question3.option3: It completely eliminated the possibility of distillation but severely degraded teacher performance

title: FlowReasoner: Reinforcing Query-Level Meta-Agents
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces FlowReasoner, a query-level meta-agent for automating the design of personalized multi-agent systems in the domain of AI agent systems.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous task-level meta-agents that create fixed workflows for specific tasks, proposing instead a query-level approach that generates a unique multi-agent system for each individual user query through reasoning-based optimization.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the limitation of existing multi-agent systems that are either manually designed (requiring significant human effort) or task-level automated (creating one-size-fits-all systems that lack adaptability to individual queries).

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors distill reasoning abilities from DeepSeek R1 to endow FlowReasoner with basic multi-agent system generation capabilities, then enhance it through reinforcement learning with external execution feedback using a multi-purpose reward focused on performance, complexity, and efficiency.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** FlowReasoner outperforms existing methods across engineering and competition code benchmarks, notably surpassing o1-mini by 10.52% accuracy across three benchmarks, while demonstrating superior adaptability by generating personalized workflows tailored to specific queries.

question1.option1: FlowReasoner uses more complex search algorithms
question1.option2: FlowReasoner generates a personalized multi-agent system for each individual user query
question1.option3: FlowReasoner requires less computational resources

question2.question: How does FlowReasoner enhance its reasoning capabilities after the initial training?
question2.option1: Through manual optimization by human experts
question2.option2: Through Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
question2.option3: Through reinforcement learning with external execution feedback

title: Learning to Reason under Off-Policy Guidance
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper focuses on enhancing large language models' reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning that integrates off-policy guidance.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on zero-RL approaches that train reasoning models using only on-policy rollouts and rule-based rewards, and proposes LUFFY, a framework that incorporates off-policy reasoning traces from stronger models to expand learning beyond the model's initial capabilities.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the limitation of existing zero-RL methods which constrain learning to a model's own outputs, preventing acquisition of reasoning abilities beyond its initial capabilities.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use a mixed-policy approach that combines off-policy demonstrations with on-policy rollouts during training, employing policy shaping via regularized importance sampling to emphasize low-probability but crucial actions.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** LUFFY achieves an average gain of over +7.0 points across six math benchmarks and +6.2 points on out-of-distribution tasks, outperforming both imitation-based supervised fine-tuning and existing zero-RL methods in both performance and generalization.

question1.question: What is the primary limitation of existing zero-RL methods that LUFFY aims to overcome?
question1.option1: High computational cost and training instability
question1.option2: Inability to learn reasoning abilities beyond the model's initial capabilities
question1.option3: Poor performance on simple mathematical problems

question2.question: How does LUFFY's policy shaping mechanism enhance learning from off-policy traces?
question2.option1: By eliminating all low-probability actions from the model's policy
question2.option2: By assigning more importance to high-probability actions only
question2.option3: By amplifying learning signals for low-probability but crucial actions

question3.question: What advantage did LUFFY demonstrate over supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in the experimental results?
question3.option1: Superior generalization capability, especially on out-of-distribution tasks
question3.option2: Significantly faster training times with less computational resources
question3.option3: Ability to completely eliminate hallucinations in mathematical reasoning

title:
StyleMe3D: Stylization with Disentangled Priors by Multiple Encoders on
  3D Gaussians
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper presents StyleMe3D, a framework for transferring artistic styles to 3D Gaussian Splatting representations while preserving geometric integrity.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and existing style transfer techniques, proposing a novel approach that integrates multi-modal style conditioning, multi-level semantic alignment, and perceptual quality enhancement.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the challenge of stylizing 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes with artistic styles while maintaining geometric details, semantic coherence, and visual harmony.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use four key components: Dynamic Style Score Distillation (DSSD) for semantic alignment, Contrastive Style Descriptor (CSD) for content-aware textures, Simultaneously Optimized Scale (SOS) for detail preservation, and 3D Gaussian Quality Assessment (3DG-QA) for aesthetic quality.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** StyleMe3D outperforms state-of-the-art methods in preserving geometric details and ensuring stylistic consistency across scenes, achieving higher PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS scores while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities.

question1.option1: Using only VGG-based feature extraction for style transfer
question1.option2: Integration of Stable Diffusion into 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization
question1.option3: Complete modification of geometry during stylization

question2.question: Which component of StyleMe3D is specifically designed to extract medium-level style descriptors for content-aware stylization?
question2.option1: Dynamic Style Score Distillation (DSSD)
question2.option2: Contrastive Style Descriptor (CSD)
question2.option3: 3D Gaussian Quality Assessment (3DG-QA)

question3.question: During the stylization process in StyleMe3D, which parameters of the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation are optimized?
question3.option1: Only the geometric parameters
question3.option2: Only the color parameters
question3.option3: Both geometric and color parameters

title: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper explores Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) for improving Large Language Models' reasoning capabilities on unlabeled data during inference time.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on Test-Time Scaling methods and reinforcement learning for reasoning, proposing a novel approach that enables LLMs to self-evolve through reinforcement learning on unlabeled test data.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the challenge of applying reinforcement learning during inference on unlabeled data without access to ground-truth information for reward estimation.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors implement TTRL by using majority voting among multiple model-generated outputs to estimate labels and compute rule-based rewards, which are then used to optimize the model through reinforcement learning.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** TTRL achieved significant performance improvements, boosting Qwen-2.5-Math-7B's pass@1 performance by approximately 159% on AIME 2024 and an average gain of 84% across mathematical reasoning benchmarks, while consistently surpassing the upper limit of the initial model's performance.

question1.question: What is the core challenge that Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) aims to solve?
question1.option1: Optimizing computational resources during model pre-training
question1.option2: Estimating rewards during inference without access to ground-truth labels
question1.option3: Generating longer chain-of-thought reasoning sequences

question2.question: What surprising phenomenon did researchers observe when applying TTRL?
question2.option1: TTRL models required less computational resources than traditional methods
question2.option2: TTRL models could surpass their own training signal and exceed the Maj@N upper bound
question2.option3: TTRL only worked on small models but failed on larger architectures

question3.question: When is TTRL most likely to fail according to the paper?
question3.option1: When applied to small datasets with fewer than 100 examples
question3.option2: When the model lacks sufficient prior knowledge on the target task
question3.option3: When the model generates outputs that are too consistent

title: Kuwain 1.5B: An Arabic SLM via Language Injection
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces Kuwain 1.5B, a small language model that enhances Arabic language capabilities through a novel injection method into an existing English-centric language model.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous work in multilingual language model adaptation but proposes a more efficient approach by injecting a new language through selective layer extension and vocabulary expansion rather than complete retraining.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses how to effectively expand a monolingual language model to support a new language (Arabic) while preserving its original language (English) capabilities without expensive retraining from scratch.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors extended TinyLlama 1.1B by adding 8 new trainable layers, expanding its vocabulary with 26K Arabic tokens while keeping original layers frozen, and training on 90 billion Arabic tokens and 20 billion English tokens.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** The approach improved Arabic language performance by 8% across various benchmarks while maintaining (and slightly improving by 1%) English language performance, achieving competitive results compared to much larger models while reducing training costs by 70%.

question1.option1: Training the entire model from scratch with both Arabic and English data
question1.option2: Adding new trainable layers while keeping original layers frozen and expanding vocabulary
question1.option3: Translating English training data into Arabic for better linguistic alignment

question2.question: What was the optimal proportion of English data needed during training to maintain the model's original capabilities?
question2.option1: 50% English data
question2.option2: 20% English data
question2.option3: 5% English data

question3.question: What happened when the authors tried to stack multiple new layers consecutively instead of distributing them throughout the model?
question3.option1: It improved Arabic performance but degraded English capabilities
question3.option2: It led to unstable training and degraded overall performance
question3.option3: It reduced training time but required more GPU memory

title: The Bitter Lesson Learned from 2,000+ Multilingual Benchmarks
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** Analysis of multilingual benchmarks in natural language processing and artificial intelligence evaluation.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** Based on previous multilingual evaluation frameworks; proposes principles for effective multilingual benchmarking and emphasizes the need for culturally authentic evaluation resources rather than just translations.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the significant disparities in how language models perform across different languages and the limitations of current multilingual evaluation practices.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** Comprehensive analysis of over 2,000 multilingual benchmarks from 148 countries published between 2021-2024, examining language distribution, task types, translation methods, and correlation with human judgments.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** Found that English remains overrepresented despite efforts to promote diversity; STEM-related tasks show stronger correlation with human judgments (0.70-0.85) than traditional NLP tasks (0.11-0.30); and localized benchmarks align better with human judgments (0.68) than translated ones (0.47).

title: DreamO: A Unified Framework for Image Customization
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces DreamO, a unified framework for image customization within the domain of generative AI and computer vision.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous task-specific image customization approaches and diffusion transformer (DiT) models, proposing a new unified framework that can handle multiple customization types simultaneously and combine different conditions.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the challenge of developing a unified framework for various image customization tasks (identity, subject, style, try-on) that can seamlessly integrate multiple conditions.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use a diffusion transformer framework with feature routing constraints, a placeholder strategy for condition placement, and a progressive three-stage training strategy on a large-scale custom dataset.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** The results demonstrate that DreamO effectively performs various image customization tasks with high quality and flexibly integrates different types of control conditions within a single model.

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of DreamO compared to previous image customization approaches?
question1.option1: It uses a completely new architecture different from diffusion models
question1.option2: It unifies multiple customization tasks in a single model with flexible condition integration
question1.option3: It requires no training data and works entirely through zero-shot learning

question2.question: What technique does DreamO use to ensure precise querying of relevant information from reference images?
question2.option1: Feature routing constraint
question2.option2: Progressive distillation
question2.option3: Gradient-based attention mapping

question3.question: How many stages are in DreamO's progressive training strategy?
question3.option1: Two stages: initial training and quality alignment
question3.option2: Three stages: initial consistency, full-scale training, and quality alignment
question3.option3: Four stages: pretraining, fine-tuning, distillation, and alignment

title:
Decoupled Global-Local Alignment for Improving Compositional
  Understanding
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces a framework called Decoupled Global-Local Alignment (DeGLA) for improving compositional understanding in vision-language models while preserving general capabilities.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on CLIP's contrastive language-image pretraining approach, proposing a new framework that addresses the limitation of previous methods which improved compositional understanding at the cost of reduced general capabilities.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper aims to solve the challenge of improving a vision-language model's compositional understanding (ability to comprehend relations and attributes) without compromising its inherent general capabilities.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use a self-distillation mechanism within global alignment to preserve general capabilities, and propose Image-Grounded Contrast and Text-Grounded Contrast losses for local alignment, supported by high-quality negative captions generated using Large Language Models.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** DeGLA achieved an average improvement of 3.5% across compositional understanding benchmarks (VALSE, SugarCrepe, ARO) while simultaneously improving zero-shot classification performance by 13.0% compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

question1.question: What is the main limitation of previous approaches that DeGLA aims to address?
question1.option1: Previous approaches were too computationally expensive for practical use
question1.option2: Previous approaches improved compositional understanding but compromised general capabilities
question1.option3: Previous approaches required too much training data to be effective

question2.question: Which mechanism does DeGLA use to retain the model's inherent general capabilities?
question2.option1: Self-distillation with a frozen teacher model from an exponential moving average
question2.option2: Transfer learning from multiple pre-trained vision models
question2.option3: Curriculum learning with gradually increasing task difficulty

question3.question: How does DeGLA generate high-quality negative captions for training?
question3.option1: By randomly shuffling words in positive captions
question3.option2: By leveraging the in-context learning capability of Large Language Models
question3.option3: By extracting incorrect captions from existing image-text datasets

title: Learning Adaptive Parallel Reasoning with Language Models
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper presents Adaptive Parallel Reasoning (APR), a framework for language models to efficiently distribute reasoning computation across both serial and parallel operations.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous reasoning approaches like chain-of-thought and self-consistency, proposing a novel method that allows language models to orchestrate both serialized and parallel computations end-to-end using spawn() and join() operations.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses limitations of existing reasoning methods where serialized approaches exhaust context windows and increase latency, while parallel methods lack coordination resulting in redundant computations.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors implemented a parent-child threading mechanism allowing language models to delegate subtasks to multiple child inference threads in parallel, and used end-to-end reinforcement learning to optimize this process without requiring predefined reasoning structures.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** APR demonstrated significant benefits on the Countdown reasoning task: higher performance within the same context window (83.4% vs. 60.0%), superior scalability with increased computation (80.1% vs. 66.6%), and improved accuracy at equivalent latency (75.2% vs. 57.3%).

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of Adaptive Parallel Reasoning (APR) compared to previous reasoning methods?
question1.option1: It uses a larger context window than previous methods
question1.option2: It enables language models to adaptively distribute computation between serial and parallel operations
question1.option3: It eliminates the need for language models completely

question2.question: In the Countdown task experiments, what did reinforcement learning primarily help APR achieve?
question2.option1: Improved decision quality within a fixed compute budget
question2.option2: Reduced the number of child threads needed
question2.option3: Scaling test-time compute by increasing both sequence length and number of child threads

question3.question: What operations does APR introduce to enable parallel reasoning?
question3.option1: pause() and continue()
question3.option2: spawn() and join()
question3.option3: fork() and merge()

title:
RefVNLI: Towards Scalable Evaluation of Subject-driven Text-to-image
  Generation
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper focuses on evaluating subject-driven text-to-image generation, which aims to generate images that match a text prompt while preserving a referenced subject's identity.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on existing evaluation metrics that separately assess textual alignment or subject preservation, proposing REFVNLI as a cost-effective metric that evaluates both aspects simultaneously without relying on expensive API calls.

3. **❓ Problem:** Current evaluation methods for subject-driven text-to-image generation either assess only one aspect of the task, correlate poorly with human judgments, or rely on costly API-based evaluation, limiting progress in the field.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors fine-tuned PaliGemma on a large-scale dataset of 1.2 million triplets (reference image, prompt, target image) automatically curated from video frames and image perturbations, with both textual alignment and subject preservation labels.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** REFVNLI consistently matches or outperforms existing baselines across multiple benchmarks and subject categories, achieving up to 6.4-point gains in textual alignment and 8.5-point gains in subject consistency, while aligning with human preferences at over 87% accuracy for rare concepts.

question1.question: What is the main innovation of REFVNLI compared to previous evaluation metrics?
question1.option1: It uses GPT-4 to evaluate images more accurately
question1.option2: It evaluates both textual alignment and subject preservation in a single prediction
question1.option3: It only focuses on rare entities and concepts

question2.question: How did the authors create negative examples for subject preservation during training?
question2.option1: By using AI-generated fake images of the subjects
question2.option2: By pairing frames from different video scenes with different subjects
question2.option3: By masking and inpainting identity-critical regions of subjects

question3.question: In which category did REFVNLI show the largest performance improvement for subject consistency?
question3.option1: Landmarks category (8.5 points gain)
question3.option2: Multi-subject setting in ImagenHub (8.5 points gain)
question3.option3: Human category in DreamBench++ (6.3 points gain)

title:
Breaking the Modality Barrier: Universal Embedding Learning with
  Multimodal LLMs
content:
1. **📘 Topic and Domain:** The paper introduces "UniME," a framework for universal embedding learning with multimodal large language models to enable cross-modal representation learning.

2. **💡 Previous Research and New Ideas:** The paper builds on previous multimodal models like CLIP and E5-V but proposes a novel two-stage framework to overcome limitations like text token truncation, isolated encoding, and deficient compositionality.

3. **❓ Problem:** The paper addresses the challenge of learning discriminative universal representations that can handle diverse multimodal tasks while maintaining compositional understanding.

4. **🛠️ Methods:** The authors use a two-stage approach: first applying textual discriminative knowledge distillation from a powerful LLM teacher model, then implementing hard negative enhanced instruction tuning with false negative filtering.

5. **📊 Results and Evaluation:** UniME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MMEB benchmark and multiple retrieval tasks, showing consistent improvements in both discriminative power and compositional understanding compared to previous models.

question1.question: What is the primary innovation of the UniME framework compared to previous multimodal embedding approaches?
question1.option1: It uses a simpler single-stage training process with fewer parameters
question1.option2: It introduces a two-stage framework with textual knowledge distillation and hard negative enhanced instruction tuning
question1.option3: It completely replaces the vision encoder with a more powerful component

question2.question: How does UniME address the problem of false negatives during training?
question2.option1: By using a similarity threshold to filter out candidates that are too similar to the query
question2.option2: By manually annotating all potential false negatives in the dataset
question2.option3: By training only on positive examples and ignoring negatives entirely

question3.question: On which type of retrieval task did UniME show the most dramatic improvement compared to previous models?
question3.option1: Short-caption retrieval tasks like Flickr30K
question3.option2: Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks
question3.option3: Compositional retrieval tasks, particularly in attribute addition
